The storage subsystem allocates, organizes, and accesses blocks on the physical storage drives.

supported idx_b8204694 by iSCSI or Fibre Channel.
The primary benefits of block storage include data redundancy and replication, which provide
fault tolerance, high performance through caching and load balancing, and maintaining data
integrity through error-checking. The low latency and high-performance data access capability

On AWS, block storage idx_0e0c1386 options include Elastic Block Store (EBS) and Instance Store. EBS
volumes idx_832fdfe2 can be attached to your Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances – virtual idx_af2d2a34 servers you
deploy in the cloud running Linux, Windows, or MacOS operating systems. EBS volumes are
network-attached, like the SAN storage option. Instance Store volumes are carved out of
physical storage attached to the host machine on which you launch your EC2 instances. Given
that EBS volumes are network attached, they can be a bit slower than Instance Store volumes.
However, EBS volumes are persistent, whereas idx_380a5fc8 Instance Store volumes only exist as long as the
EC2 instance (virtual server) is in the running state. Once the instance is stopped, the Instance
Store volume is destroyed. For these reasons, Instance Store volumes are considered temporary
storage.
File storage
File Storage is another storage idx_15395d36 architecture in which your data is organized and managed as
files within a hierarchical directory (folder) structure. You can think of file storage as
organizing your filing cabinet with folders and sub-folders within which your documents
reside.
The data structure uses file idx_353a403c systems like NFS (Network File System) or SMB/CIFS (Server
Message Block/Common Internet File System) to store, organize, and retrieve your data.
Using protocols like idx_b8b88c81 NFS and SMB, you can create file shares, making it easy to share your data.
Applications running on your virtual servers in the cloud can use file storage to share data too.
Retrieval of your data requires you to know the unique path and name within the directory
structure and identify the folders (and sub-folders, if necessary) to access the file.
Due to the nature of file storage, metadata (information used to describe the data) may be
limited. In addition, due to operating system limitations, you might experience performance
issues if your directory hierarchy runs through deeply nested subdirectories. Other
performance issues result from introduced latency when accessing files over a network, which
is usually slower than block storage.
It is also essential to appreciate that file storage represents a higher layer of abstraction above
block storage. Ultimately, all data is stored on block devices, such as direct-attached storage or
network-attached devices.
File storage is handy for file sharing, media storage and streaming, collaboration, and
document management.

volumes. Instead, the file system will grow as you add data and shrink as you delete
data, ensuring cost optimization.

compute-intensive workloads. It is designed to handle large datasets up to petabytes in

(Amazon Simple Storage Service), allowing easy import and export of data between
Amazon S3 and the Luster File System. Amazon S3 can be used to store data, and when
you need to process it, you can import it into FSx for Luster. It is ideal for workloads
idx_be5ba496 such as machine learning, big data analytics, and high-performance computing (HPC)
applications.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: This service offers Microsoft Windows-based
EC2 instances file-sharing idx_1075d0cc capabilities. The service runs on fully managed Windows-
based servers in the background. It requires the presence of Microsoft Active Directory

Windows-based file-sharing solution in the AWS cloud.
Object storage
Object storage is designed especially for idx_3cdc80f6 cloud storage applications. The architecture presents a
flat-file structure and stores your data as objects in their entirety, with extensive metadata
information and globally unique identifiers, making them ideal for storing structured, semi-
structured, or unstructured data types. Due to its flat file structure, there are no folders or
directories to manage. This also means you avoid the limitations of extensively nested
directories, which affect performance and scalability.
The architecture lends itself to horizontal scaling, which involves adding more nodes to your
storage pool. This means you can store virtually unlimited amounts of data, making it ideal for
data lakes, big data, large files, and more.
Access to your data can be done using API calls (e.g., RESTful APIs), and this makes object
storage ideal for web-based applications by allowing access from anywhere over the Internet.
Many companies use object storage to host digital assets such as media files (images, video,
and documents) since object storage is much cheaper than file storage solutions.

While object storage solutions offer high scalability and almost unlimited data storage, they
have certain limitations. These include higher latency than file storage systems, especially
when accessing small files and applications requiring frequent read/write operations.
Like file storage, object storage presents an abstraction layer for the underlying block devices,
and this presents performance overhead due to the need to process metadata and API calls.
Other disadvantages of object storage include limitations on individual object sizes (Amazon
S3 has a maximum object size of 50TB). Also, while the flat file namespace makes storing
almost unlimited amounts of data easy, it is less intuitive than the file-folder hierarchical
structure of file storage solutions. You also cannot host applications or databases on Amazon
S3 due to its higher latency issues and lack of computing capability.
AWS offers Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), an object storage solution that allows
you to store almost unlimited amounts of data cost-effectively. With Amazon S3, you create
buckets (containers) and place your objects in a flat file structure. You can then access your
data via the web console, through the CLI, or idx_084224b2 programmatically by making API calls.
In the next section, you will learn more about Amazon S3 and its core features.
Working with Amazon S3
Amazon S3 is one of AWS's most popular products, offering a robust, highly durable, scalable,
and cost-effective object idx_305b47ce storage solution. With Amazon S3, customers can store almost
unlimited amounts of data at a fraction of the cost compared to hosting a similar solution on
premises.
Amazon S3 is designed to offer 99.999999999% (that's eleven 9s) of durability. This means
that if you store 10,000,000 objects in Amazon S3, then on average, you might expect to
experience the loss of a single object every 10,000 years. This is possible because your data is
replicated across multiple storage devices and availability zones within a given region. Another
critical factor is that while AWS will replicate your data across multiple availability zones in
the region you host it, it will never replicate data to other regions unless you configure it to do
so. This ensures you can maintain data privacy and sovereignty if such regulatory requirements
bind your business.
In the next section, you will learn more about Amazon S3 buckets and objects—the nuts and
bolts of the product.
Buckets and objects
Buckets are containers you create in Amazon S3 that can host unlimited objects in the cloud.
You can have up to 100 buckets per AWS account. However, this is just a soft limit and can
always be increased to 1,000 buckets by getting idx_43cbb131 approval from the AWS support team.

Buckets traditionally have a globally unique namespace – a feature that enables them to be

As previously discussed, Amazon S3 is an object storage solution with a flat file structure. This
means that objects are ultimately idx_fc150096 stored in the root of the bucket without a real directory-style
hierarchical structure. This can make navigating and traversing objects in the bucket
cumbersome, especially if you have hundreds or thousands of them.
Amazon S3 offers a solution idx_517dd65d using prefixes and delimiters, which can help you manage and
browse your objects in a idx_9b57f08f simulated hierarchical fashion. This allows you to create a path-like

While this architecture allows you to better manage your objects, the fact is that the keys of the
object itself now comprise prefixes and delimiters. For example, the version 3 recipe of the
raspberry kombucha now has a key (name) of current-recipes/ raspberry ‑ kombucha ‑ v3.doc.
Ultimately, all objects are stored in a flat file structure. One exception to this is when using a
particular bucket type called an idx_54144972 S3 directory bucket, discussed later in this chapter.
One benefit of using prefixes and delimiters is that they help you limit search results to only
those keys that begin with a specific prefix. This allows you to perform list operations such that
keys with a common prefix are returned as a single result, reducing the number of requests
made and saving on cost.
Prefixes can also enhance performance when you access objects. Amazon S3 offers 2,500 PUT/
COPY/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD operations per second per prefix. By using prefixes to
categorize your objects, you can increase overall performance. For example, if you have five
prefixes to categorize five different collections of objects, you can achieve a total read
performance of 27,500 (5,500 * 5) read requests per second for your GET operations.
As an organization, you may have different data sets with varying access patterns. For example,
you may have a subset of data that you need to access frequently and another set of data that
you just want to store as archives, accessing them only on rare occasions. Furthermore, you
may also have some data sets where the access pattern is difficult to predict. AWS offers
storage classes for such varying use cases, which are discussed in the next section.
131 Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)
Choosing the right Amazon S3 storage class
With Amazon S3, you can store idx_6252c101 unlimited data in an S3 bucket. However, not all data is idx_608800a3 treated
the same. Usually, only a subset of data tends to be accessed very frequently. Some data sets
must be accessed instantly, especially with applications that are sensitive to latency. Other
data sets are stored for archival purposes, where instant access is not required. As an example,
the graphics design team at Belly Brew Co. Limited creates certain digital assets for its monthly
online newsletters, comprising documents, images, and videos. This month's newsletter
webpage will need instant access to those digital assets so that when end users access the
webpage, those digital assets are rendered with the website. Since the webpage only
showcases the current month's newsletter, previously used digital assets for previous months'
newsletters do not need to be instantly accessible. However, the company may still choose to
store them for reference.

The following provides a summary of the various storage classes on AWS:
Storage classes designed for frequently accessed data
If you need instant access to your data with millisecond latency and you will be making
frequent requests for your data, then the following idx_4d563894 storage class is recommended:
Amazon S3 Standard: This is the default storage class offering millisecond latency for
applications that require instant access. Examples include web applications. Data is
always replicated across at least three availability zones, and you get 99.99%
availability. Unlike other infrequent access storage classes, you are not charged a
retrieval fee, which makes this class ideal for frequently accessed data.
Amazon S3 Express One-Zone: As of 2026, this is one of the latest storage classes
added to the Amazon S3 service. Data is stored in a single availability zone of your
choice, designed to deliver single-digit millisecond access. This is further made
possible because you can place your compute resources in the same availability zones
as the bucket, reducing the physical distance between the two types of resources. It is
specially designed for idx_2e7e912d latency-sensitive applications and uses a particular bucket type
known as the S3 directory bucket. Unlike standard S3 buckets, which store objects as
flat files, this newer bucket type organizes data into a directory hierarchy that can scale
horizontally. It also isn't affected by the current prefix limitations.
Reduced Redundancy (RRS): This storage class is designed for reproducible
noncritical data, such as thumbnail images or idx_89328f6e larger original images you might use for
your YouTube video chapters. Amazon no longer recommends using this storage class
because while it offers the same availability as the Standard storage class, it only
provides 99.99% (that's four 9s) of durability.
Storage classes designed for infrequently accessed data
These two storage classes are cheaper than the Amazon S3 Standard class because they are
designed for infrequently accessed data idx_a84215f9 while offering millisecond latency access. AWS
understands that customers may have a vast collection of data they seldom access, but one
that requires instant access when needed. AWS offers them a lower price point for not
frequently accessing this data. To deter customers from misusing this storage class and ensure
they are used for infrequent access only, AWS enforces an object retrieval cost. In addition,

Amazon S3 One Zone-IA (Infrequent Access): This storage class is cheaper than the

secondary backup copies of your data.
Storage classes designed for archival or rarely accessed data
AWS offers three classes designed for long-term (archival) storage requirements. In return, you
pay less to host your data in Amazon S3. These idx_22c63814 storage classes are cost-effective if you use them
as intended – rarely accessing your data and storing it for a longer term. However, you still get
the same levels of durability.
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (IR): Although you may rarely access data hosted in this
storage class, you might still need instant access to it. This storage class offers
millisecond retrieval for your critical data when you needed most. However, the
minimum storage duration is 90 days. If you store data for less than this, you are
charged for the entire 90-day period.
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: This storage class is cheaper than Glacier IR since data is
not instantly available. It is designed for data you may need to retrieve once or twice a
year. There is a 90-day minimum storage period and a retrieval fee. You must follow a
retrieval process, which can take some time, ranging from minutes to hours, depending
on the retrieval tier you choose, as follows:
Expedited retrieval: This is designed to retrieve a subset of your data within 1 to
5 minutes. You can use this tier when you urgently must get access to archival
data, which is the most expensive of the tiers.
Standard retrieval: This is designed for objects that need to be restored within a
3-to-5-hour window. This tier is cheaper than Expedited retrieval.
Bulk retrieval: This tier is designed for customers who have massive data sets
and can take 5 to 12 hours. There is no retrieval fee for this tier.

attached to the resource, such as an S3 bucket. With idx_8add8c2f Amazon S3, resource-based policies are

Amazon S3 versioning
You may often have multiple copies of idx_01f59f39 your data, such as documents you update regularly. If
you make changes to an object (such as a document) and upload it to an Amazon S3 bucket
using the same Key (name), it overwrites the previous copy of that object. This is because the
versioning feature is not enabled by default. If you need to protect earlier copies of your data as
you regularly perform updates, you can enable versioning. This adds a version ID to every
upload action idx_e71827e9 you perform for that object, effectively creating a new version of it.
You can then access previous versions of the same object and restore them if there is an issue
with the current version or refer to earlier versions as required. With versioning enabled, you
also mitigate the risk of accidental deletions. This is because if you perform a standard delete
operation without specifying the version ID of a particular object version, Amazon S3 doesn't
delete the object; it simply hides the object from view in the management console by adding a
delete marker to the object. You can then restore the object to view by deleting the delete
marker.
Versioning must be used carefully as it incurs additional costs due to increased storage
consumption.
While versioning can help you prevent accidental deletions and allow you to maintain multiple
versions of an object, it cannot prevent issues that might cause the bucket to get deleted, or if
there is a regional disaster in which the bucket is hosted. To address such concerns, AWS also
offers another feature called Cross-Region Replication, which is discussed next.
Cross-region and same-region replication
As discussed previously, AWS will never idx_8771ed47 replicate objects hosted in one region to another
region to ensure that you abide by any regulatory or data sovereignty laws. However, nothing
can stop you from replicating objects across regions if your business use case requires it idx_72310540 and if

Customers can idx_1289c7e7 configure Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to copy objects from buckets in one
region to another asynchronously. If idx_fda66fb9 required, you can also set up bidirectional replication,
ensuring your buckets are always in sync. CRR can be used for the following use cases:
Reduce latency: You can reduce latency by copying objects to buckets located in
regions closer to end users. This is particularly noticeable with huge files, and if you do
not make use of a content delivery network such as Amazon CloudFront (discussed
later in Chapter 11).
Increase operational efficiency: If you have applications that need to interact with
the data in your Amazon S3 bucket, placing those buckets closer to where you host your
application will increase operational efficiency. This also means that if you host your
applications across multiple regions, a copy of the data in each area would be
beneficial. Cross-regional replication can make it extremely easy to ensure that your
application has fast and reliable access to data when needed.
Fulfil regulatory or compliance requirements: Your organization may need to
comply with regulatory requirements that stipulate a copy of your data is hosted in
another region to ensure security against any major disasters. Cross-region replication
can help fulfill this requirement very easily.
Interestingly, you can also configure bucket replication across buckets hosted in the same
region. This is known as Same-Region Replication (SRR). Often, companies idx_d159fd93 may wish to
implement SRR for use cases such as log aggregation, replicating data between development
and testing environments, or across AWS accounts. You may also be required to set up SRR for
your buckets for compliance requirements and protection from accidental bucket deletions.
A prerequisite to configuring bucket replication is that you must also enable versioning.
Finally, you can replicate objects between two buckets, where the replicas are stored in a
different storage class in the destination bucket than the original data in the source bucket.
This can help you reduce your overall costs, where you might have the original data in Amazon
S3 Standard but the replicas in Amazon S3 Standard-IA.

To help you better manage your data lifecycle, AWS offers the Lifecycle Management feature.

previous versions.

Encryption converts data into a coded format to prevent unauthorized access, ensuring that
only those with the correct decryption key idx_df86410e can read the original information. It is widely used
in cybersecurity to protect sensitive data during storage or transmission.
Data encryption must be performed both in transit (in-flight between two systems) using
protocols like Secure Socket Layer/Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS), and at rest (while it
resides on a storage idx_1b66f723 medium such as a hard drive).

Client-side encryption: This option involves encrypting your data on the client-side
and then uploading the encrypted data to Amazon S3. You handle the full encryption

resources on-premises to the cloud. Your on-premises workloads can then work directly with
cloud storage, uploading and downloading data as required.

virtual private network (VPN) tunnels or AWS Direct Connect.

Summary
Amazon S3 is an object storage offering from AWS that comes with a vast array of features to
help businesses manage their entire data. The architecture means that it can offer
99.999999999% (eleven 9s) of durability and extremely high levels of availability, depending
on the storage class you store your data in.
In this chapter, you learned about the features of Amazon S3, including how to secure your
data with bucket policies and encryption options—a critical requirement for every business
that wishes to consider cloud storage to host their data. This chapter also includes crucial
topics you are likely to be tested on in the exam, such as how versioning can help prevent
accidental deletions and how cross-region replication can facilitate ensuring your data is closer
to end consumers. You also learned how lifecycle management can help you manage the
lifecycle of your data effectively and also optimize cost savings for the organization.
Amazon S3 offers static website hosting, a service that powers millions of websites and is
suitable for many use cases. Using Amazon S3 to host your front-end website can also help you
architect serverless solutions, which you will learn more about as you progress through this
study guide.
The chapter also discusses the AWS Storage Gateway Service, enabling you to build hybrid
cloud storage solutions for your business requirements. With options for managing files
directly in Amazon S3 from local on-premises file gateways through to continuing your backup
solutions with the tape gateway, this service ensures you can have access to cloud data with
low-latency access.
Finally, you learn about the AWS Snow Family, a service that extends edge storage and
compute services and enables you to transfer petabyte-scale data to AWS quickly.

AWS Networking Services, Part
1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
In the information technology (IT) world, networking technologies have been pivotal in
connecting our world. With this technology and its fundamental principles and processes, the
Internet as we know it came into existence.
Businesses, from home office start-ups to large multinationals, depend on this vital IT service
to communicate within their organizations and with external entities such as partners,
suppliers, and customers. Without networking, your colleague sitting a few desks away from
you would have to save a file to a disk and then pass that disk to you so you can insert it into
your computer to access a file you are collaborating on. This would be highly inefficient.
Instead, with networking, you and your colleague can save and access the file in a shared
location on a local network or even on the Internet.
Networking does more than enable devices to communicate with each other. IT networks
represent boundaries of communications, such that devices within a network are free to
communicate with each other, but access to and from external networks can be restricted.
Networks can be configured to communicate with other networks – that's how the Internet
works. It's a collection of many small networks, all interconnected. The term "Internet" itself
comes from "inter-networking." These smaller networks, which may belong to different
organizations, individuals, or service providers, connect using standardized communication
protocols such as TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol).
In this chapter, you will learn how IT networks play a fundamental role in enabling different
resources (devices) that host various parts of your application to communicate with each
other. Specifically, you will learn how to create cloud networks in your AWS account called
Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to host and manage your application resources. Amazon VPCs
are designed to help you build secure networks in the cloud within which you can host your
application resources and define exactly how they are accessed from the Internet or via private
connections from your on-premises locations. Depending on your use case, your resources,
such as web servers, application servers, and databases, may require access to and from the
Internet. You will learn how to build secure VPCs that ensure only specific authorized traffic is
permitted into and out of your VPC. This chapter will also provide a deep-dive analysis of how

While the SOHO network depicted in Figure 7.1 is simple, networks can get very complex
depending on the number of devices they need to support and the use case. The following
section provides a high-level overview of a typical business network architecture.
Basic corporate networks
Most businesses must host idx_6899b684 more complex networks with extra security in mind. This is
because a company will host several applications, some of which might be more sensitive than
others and require isolation and separation. Furthermore, the business must serve different
departments, external users, and customers. You would not want your customers getting
access to your staff payroll application now, would you? To ensure higher levels of security and
163 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
isolation of workloads, business networks are often divided into small, separate networks
designed for specific use cases.
A high-level example of such a network is illustrated in the following diagram in Figure 7.2:
Figure 7.2: Example of corporate network
As depicted in Figure 7.2, the corporate network has several small sub-networks. These small
sub-networks are also known as virtual local area networks or vLANs. These virtual LANs are
designed to isolate workloads but allow inbound idx_dce216e4 and outbound communication from other
vLANs over specific types of idx_a6f0bd10 traffic if required. Networks tend to experience a lot of traffic,
usually in the form of broadcast traffic. Broadcast traffic is a type of network communication
where a message is sent to all devices in a specific network. Think of it like someone shouting a
message in a room full of people; everyone hears it, even if it's not meant for them.
For example, when a device connects to a network and asks, "Who is the main server?" it uses
broadcast traffic to send that question to all devices. Only the correct device (the server) will
respond, but everyone else still hears the question.
Broadcasts are beneficial in small networks but can cause congestion in larger ones if overused,
like shouting in a crowded space all the time. By placing workloads in isolated virtual
networks, you can define what traffic is permitted inbound from other networks, reducing this
noise. This also helps you separate workloads unrelated to each other to enhance security and
enforce compliance.

Explaining IP addressing and subnet masks
By now, you know that network idx_b81c18a7 devices such as laptops, desktops, phones, tablets, and
printers can communicate if placed in a network that allows connectivity over a wired or
wireless connection. In addition to this physical connectivity, each device requires a unique IP
address to communicate. In the same way, as you cannot have the same mobile number used
on two separate smartphones simultaneously, you cannot have two network devices with the
same IP address communicate in the same network.
However, IP addresses do more than act as telephone numbers for your devices. IP addresses
allow you to create the network logically. This means that even if you have devices connected
physically, say over a wired/wireless connection, it's how the IP address is configured on those
devices that allows the communication to occur. As per the following diagram, even though
the laptop and desktop computers are in the same physical network, they cannot communicate
because their IP addresses are not in the same logical network. This ability to build logical
networks within a physically connected space allows you to create separate virtual LANs, as
discussed earlier.
This is all thanks to Subnet Masks, which enable idx_60a9bf8e you to define smaller logical networks within
the larger physical network. Before examining how subnet masks are used to build logical sub-

of IP addresses: IPv4 and IPv6. These are discussed in the next section.

IP address version 4 (IPv4)
The standard IP address you might be familiar idx_92e4ad05 with is IPv4. This was the first general release IP
addressing system and took the form of four decimal numbers separated by dots. An
example of an IPv4 address is 192.168.1.7. Each decimal notation is called an octet, ranging
between 0 and 255 in decimal. Computers, however, use binary numbers to communicate. This
is a base 2 number comprising only zeros and ones. Thus, the IP address you are familiar with
must be converted into binary for your computer.
Each octet in your IP Address represents 8 bits in binary, which can range from eight zeros to
eight ones (00000000 to 11111111). Since there are four octets, an IPv4 address comprises 32 bits
in binary (8 bits x 4 octets).
Take the example of the IP address 192.16.1.7. In binary, each octet would be converted into 8
bits of zeros and ones, depending on the value of the octet. The following diagram in Figure
illustrates what this IP address looks like as a binary representation.
Figure 7.3: IP address represented as binary bits
Understanding the fundamentals of IP addressing and how this conversion to binary takes
place will help you appreciate how logical networks are built. Take the example of the IP
address 192.168.1.7. Conversion idx_34487757 of this IP address to its binary equivalent requires knowing
the place value of each binary bit in decimal. The position of each bit in the octet represents a
power of 2, starting with '0' at the far right and ending with '7' at the far left of each octet.
To illustrate this conversion, let's take the last octet of the IP address 192.168.1.7, which is '7'
in this case. To convert this number into binary, start by reviewing the following table to
identify the placeholder values of each bit in binary:

Since there are only 8 bits in binary per octet, the maximum place value for the far left bit you
can define is 2 to the power of 7 (2^7). This is because you start at 2 to the power of 0 (2^0) in
the far right.
Starting from the right and idx_1537af43 moving to the left, the value of each bit can be either a '0' or the
resulting power of 2 in decimal, based on the bit position. So, for example:
The first value of the first bit is either equal to '0' or '1'. If X is 1, it is 2 to the power of 0
(2^0), which is 1.
The second bit is double the first bit and is either equal to '0' or '2'. If X is 1, it is 2 to the
power of 1 (2 ^ 1), which is 2.
The third bit is double the second bit and is either equal to '0' or '4'. If X is 1, then it is 2
to the power 2 (2 ^ 2), which is 4.
The fourth bit is double the third bit and is either equal to '0' or '8'. If X is 1, then it is 2
to the power of 3 (2^3), which is 8, and so on.
To calculate the decimal values of the binary representation, you must first identify which of
the Xs should be converted to a '1' and which to '0' in binary. The decimal value is then derived

Decimal = (X*128) + (X*64) + (X*32) + (X*16) + (X*8) + (X*4) + (X*2) + (X*1)
So, to calculate the binary representation of '7' from the IP address 192.168.1.7, you must
identify which of the 'Xs' should be converted to zeros and which ones to ones. You can only
convert those bits to ones whose value will be equal to or less than your decimal number.

As previously mentioned, the IPv4 address space comprises 32 bits. This means that the
maximum number of IP addresses in this version is 2^32, giving you 4,294,967,296 IP
addresses. On the surface, you might idx_dd65dc22 assume that this is a large number of IP addresses.
However, almost every device is now connected to a network, including the Internet. These

include your home computers, laptops, printers, scanners, and smart devices like your
doorbell. You would agree that these 4 billion odd IP addresses are insufficient.
The largest network is the Internet, and every device that must connect to the Internet must
have a unique IP address. However, an important fact is that while billions of devices must
connect to the Internet, users and applications on the Internet do not need to connect to those
devices directly. As depicted earlier in Figure 7.2, the desktops and laptops in the EUC vLAN
may require internet access, but you wouldn't want strangers on the Internet connecting to the
devices from the Internet inbound.
Realizing this simple fact, the idx_be028404 Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) devised a brilliant
plan to allocate a range of IP addresses for private use only. These IP ranges are not routable
over the Internet, which means you cannot connect to them directly from the Internet.
Businesses and homes can use these private IP address ranges to configure their internal
private networks. Since these networks are private, you can use the same set of ranges across
all businesses and homes without worrying about conflicting IP addresses.
The IANA has defined the following IP address ranges for private use:
10.0.0.0/8: IP address range: 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255
172.16.0.0/12: IP address range: 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255
192.168.0.0/16: IP address range: 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255
An additional IP Address range designed for internal networks that host devices running the
Microsoft Windows Operating System is the Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA) range.
This is particularly useful if you do not configure your internal devices with any of the private
IP address ranges mentioned earlier. This range is from 169.254.0.0 to 169.254.255.255
The remaining address ranges are considered public addresses and are considered routable
over the Internet with certain exceptions.
The key benefit of these private IP address ranges can be illustrated in the following illustration
in Figure 7.6:

As depicted in Figure 7.6, you will note that all three companies have allocated the same range

since these businesses are not connected. This also means that companies can use this private
IP address range for their idx_c5b89f15 internal networks, saving the scarce public ranges for only those
devices that need to route traffic over the Internet. Furthermore, given that these private
ranges are not routable over the Internet, it enhances your internal network security. A user on

the Internet cannot connect to the IP address 10.0.1.7, for example, since the traffic to this

The next question is obvious: if these IP address ranges are not routable on the Internet, then
how can these devices access the Internet? Most devices in your corporate network will need
Internet access, if only to download updates and patches like updated anti-virus definitions or
software. The following section explains how these devices can access the internet.
Secure internet access
In Figure 7.6, it was discussed that businesses can use private IP address ranges that are not
routable over the Internet, which offers enhanced security and enables the conservation of
public IP addresses. However, businesses still need Internet access. Almost every network
device will need some Internet access for a wide range of use cases. For example, a staff
member may want to browse the Internet or send idx_a362875f and receive emails. To enable this Internet
access, public IP addresses would be required. However, assigning devices in the internal
network with public IP addresses would defeat the purpose of the private IP address ranges
defined by the IANA.

Instead of exposing internal devices such as laptops, desktops, printers, etc., by giving them
public IP addresses, you could configure a relay device that would allow internal devices to
access the Internet through it in a manner that ensures only that relay device would require a
public IP address. This idx_3dc0cf49 device (or software application) is known as Network Address
Translation, or NAT for short.
In the following illustration in Figure 7.7, internal devices across the three companies can now
access the Internet using NAT service, which can be configured on a router that offers this
capability. The NAT device maintains an internal table of requests from internal devices to
services on the Internet and forwards that traffic, advertising only its public IP address.
Responses are received by the NAT device, which are then relayed back to the original
requester, as depicted for Company A in the diagram, where the client machine with private IP
192.168.1.8 needs to access the AWS platform. The response from the platform would be sent
to the NAT device, which would then relay it back to the client machine.
Figure 7.7: Private IP address ranges businesses use with Internet access via NAT services
As per Figure 7.7, network devices such as computers can access the internet without a public
IP address. The NAT device idx_264f905c maintains a table to ensure that responses to any Internet-hosted
resource can be relayed to the correct device.
While private IP address ranges have enabled billions of devices to access the Internet, it is not
a permanent solution. More and more devices now need direct Internet access, and a revision
of the IPv4 address scheme was essential. This idx_ef89cf31 led to the development of IPv6 (Internet
Protocol version 6) by idx_20f70945 the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) in the 1990s. The
following section provides a high-level overview of this newer version.
171 AWS Networking Services, Part 1 – Virtual Private Cloud (VPCs)
Overview of IPv6
The IETF designed a new version of the idx_1b5f4134 IP Address system known as IPv6. This version uses a
128-bit addressing system, giving you 2^128 addresses. This is enormous, far exceeding the 4.3
billion addresses in IPv4 (2^32). IPv6 addresses are denoted in hexadecimal format rather than
standard decimal since the numbering system would be very long. This newer version can
ensure that every device on Earth (and beyond) can have a unique address, allowing for better
scalability, security, and efficiency in networking.
While IPv6 is the answer to the drawbacks in IPv4, most networks still need to be able to use
the older version of IP addressing, partly due to compatibility and interoperability with legacy
devices that may not be IPv6-aware.
An important concept is that idx_20902745 networks often need to be isolated. Network boundaries ensure

chunks.heading: Chapter 7 170
chunks.content:
the isolation and separation of networks, usually required for security, compliance, and
operational efficiency. Furthermore, networks can be of varying sizes, determining how many
devices can be hosted in that network. These concepts are discussed in detail in the following
section.
Comparing network sizes and IP address classes
The IETF designed different classes of IPv4 addresses to help cater to various network sizes and
use cases. Initially, there were five classes defined. This idx_4fe06d1c was known as the classful addressing
scheme. Classes A to C represent idx_d3fd7a3d generic unicast IP addresses (with certain exceptions). A
unicast IP address uniquely identifies a single device on a network, allowing direct one-to-one
communication.
Class D comprises multicast addresses. A multicast IP address sends data to multiple devices
simultaneously within a specific group rather than to a single destination. Class D (224.0.0.0
to 239.255.255.255) is reserved for multicast traffic in IPv4, enabling efficient group
communication. This is ideal for idx_766d9b30 applications like live video streaming (e.g., IPTV or video
conferencing), where data needs to be efficiently delivered to multiple recipients
simultaneously using multicast. Class E (240.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255) is reserved for
experimental and future use in IPv4 and is not typically assigned for standard networking.
Classes A to C define standard network sizes. This is achieved by masking a portion of the IP
address to represent the network. This also ensures your ability to create isolated networks
that cannot directly communicate with each other unless you add a routing mechanism
between the two networks.

The following standard classes have the following configurations:
Class A: The first octet (first 8 bits) of a class A address represents the network portion,
where the remaining three octets (24 bits) define the host portion. Furthermore, the
first bit of a Class A network is always set to '0' in binary since the IP range for a Class A
starts at '0'. The remaining 7 bits in the first octet define the number of networks idx_a548ff32 in this
class. Thus, taking 2 to the power of 7 (2^7) will give you 128, the total number of
possible networks you can have in a Class A. It is important to remember that two
networks within this range cannot be used to host devices. The first network is
0.0.0.0, and the second is 127.0.0.0 (up to 127.255.255.255). This is because:
0.0.0.0 represents a reference point rather than a network. It means a default
route and is used to signify any network, like a wildcard for routing purposes.
127.0.0.0 is known as the loopback address and is used for local communication
within a device. Any data packet sent to 127.x.x.x never leaves the device – it is
often used for troubleshooting or testing applications locally.
The total number of possible host machines in a Class A network is calculated as
follows: (2^24) - 2 = 16,777,214. You must subtract 2 IP addresses because the first IP
address represents the network ID, and the last IP address represents the broadcast IP.
Class B: The first two octets (first 16 bits) of a class B address define the network
portion, and the remaining 16 bits can be used for the host portion. The first two bits
are also set to 10 in a class B network, meaning that this class's starting IP address is
128. This means the remaining 14 bits (16 minus the two bits set to '10') define the
number of networks in a Class B range. Therefore, the total possible networks you can
have in a Class B is 16,384 (2^14).
The remaining 16 bits are used for possible host IP addresses and are calculated as
follows: (2^16) - 2 = 65,534. You must subtract 2 IP addresses because the first IP
address represents the network ID, and the last IP address represents the broadcast IP
address per network in this class.
Class C: The first three idx_61bf82d4 octets (first 24 bits) of a Class C address define the network
portion, and the remaining 8 bits represent the host portion. In a Class C network, the
first three far-left bits are set to 110, meaning that this class's starting range of IP
addresses is 192. Furthermore, the remaining 21 bits define the number of networks in a
Class C. This gives you 2,097,152 (2 ^ 21) possible networks.
The remaining 8 bits are used for possible host IP addresses and are calculated as
follows: (2^8) - 2 = 254. Again, remember that the first IP address in the network is the
network ID, and the last IP address is used for broadcast traffic.

These IP addresses were originally assigned strictly according to classful network design
architecture. However, this approach came with severe limitations, such as the inability to
create custom network sizes. With the scarcity of public IP addresses, classful network design
proved inefficient. For instance, a small company might only need one public IP address to
enable its internal network of users to access the Internet via a NAT device. With classful
networks, they would be compelled to be assigned a Class C address at a minimum, providing
the business with 254 public IP addresses, which represents a complete waste of this scarce
resource.
An alternative solution that was devised is the classless interdomain routing system (CIDR),
which allows you to build custom network sizes and subnetworks. Before looking at how
custom network sizes can be built, it is idx_f3c2abea essential to understand how these networks are created
using the IP addressing system. For example, how can an IP address 192.168.6.8 be on a
different network than 172.31.5.4? This is all thanks to masking an IP address into a network
portion and a host portion using Subnet Masks, which is the topic of the next section.
What are subnet masks?
A subnet mask is a 32-bit number like an IP address. However, subnet masks mask an IP
address to determine which portion of an IP address idx_79d0d3de belongs to the network and which

Chapter 7 174
portion belongs to the hosts. Ultimately, subnet masks are thus used to define network
boundaries and the number of IP addresses per network. This allows you to use subnet masks
to create standard classful networks, as previously discussed, as well as custom network sizes
and sub-networks.
A subnet mask consists of two parts:
Network Portion (set to 1s) → Identifies the network
Host Portion (set to 0s) → Identifies the specific hosts within the network
The decimal notation of a subnet mask range is 255.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255. A logical AND
operation is performed between an IP address and a chosen subnet mask to determine the
network it belongs to. Devices on the same network using the same subnet mask can
communicate with each other freely, whereas communication with other networks would
require some form of traffic routing. This allows you to isolate traffic between different
networks and enhance security.
The Class A, B, and C networks are created using a set of standard subnet masks. Based on
earlier discussion, you would guess that the IP address 10.0.0.5 belongs to a Class A network,
since the first octet '10' falls within the 0–127 IP address range. However, using subnet masks,
you can define an IP address such as 10.0.0.5 as part of a Class B network instead. This is
achieved by using an appropriate subnet mask to mask off the first two octets for the network
portion and the remaining two octets to represent the host portion, which, as you now know, is
a standard Class B configuration.
For example, take the IP address 10.0.0.5. If you associate it with a subnet mask of

Now, while subnet masks can help define different network sizes and identify which IPs belong
to which network, often you may wish to divide a larger network into small sub-networks, as
previously discussed in the idx_39c7c62b section 'Basic Corporate Networks' and depicted in Figure 7.2. To
achieve this, you would use subnet masks to divide existing networks further into small
networks through a process known as subnetting, which will be discussed in the next section.
What is subnetting?
Previously, you used fixed-length subnet idx_0453ceb4 masks to mask off portions of your IP address to
define network and host portions. You would mask off the first octet of the IP address for a
Class A network, the first two octets for a Class B network, and the first three octets for a Class
C network. So, for a class A network, you could use the subnet mask 255.0.0.0 to mask off the
first octet of your IP address for the network portion. Any changes in the first octet of an IP
address would yield a different network. For example, when using a subnet mask of 255.0.0.0,
the IP address 10.0.0.0 is on a different network than 31.0.0.0.
Subnetting is a process by which you can use a subnet mask to divide a more extensive network
into smaller subnetworks (subnets). This is particularly useful when you have different workload
types that need to be isolated from each other, or you want to reduce broadcast traffic,
allowing only permitted network connections between these workloads. For example, you
have a more extensive corporate network and want subnetworks for your backend databases,
frontend web servers, and a network for your employee workforce.
Subnetting involves borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address range to create these
smaller subnetworks. These borrowed bits effectively enable you to create subsets of your
larger primary network. The subnetworks are therefore part of the larger primary network, but
traffic between the subnetworks can be restricted to ensure isolation of workloads, enhance
security, and ensure operational efficiency.
Take the example of a business that needs eight subnetworks, each capable of hosting 30 IP
addresses for a maximum of 30 devices idx_109f3352 per network. The company could use a standard Class
C IP address range of 192.168.0.0, with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. The resulting eight
networks could be:
Network 1: 192.168.1.0 (subnet mask: 255.255.255.0)
Network 2: 192.168.2.0 (subnet mask: 255.255.255.0)
Network 3: 192.168.3.0 (subnet mask: 255.255.255.0)

Network 5: 192.168.5.0 (subnet mask: 255.255.255.0)
Network 6: 192.168.6.0 (subnet mask: 255.255.255.0)
